subject: math
title: Grade 4 Money and Making Change
seo_title: Grade 4 Money and Making Change Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Financial literacy – monetary calculations, including making change with amounts to 100 dollars and making simple financial decisions
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on money for the BC curriculum: count Canadian coins and bills to $100, make amounts with the fewest coins, make change by counting up, round cash totals to the nearest 5¢, and choose the better buy or plan to save. 100 questions with an answer key, good FSA numeracy practice.
key_big: To make change, count up from the price to the money paid: $7.65 → $7.70 → $8 → $10 is 5¢ + 30¢ + $2 = $2.35.
key_sub: Cash totals round to the nearest 5¢ because Canada has no pennies; card payments are exact. A quarter is 25¢, and 125¢ in coins is $1.25.
body_html:
Canadian coins and bills

Know each coin by its value, not its size. The dime is the smallest coin, but it is worth more than the nickel. Canada has no pennies.

Count money: bills first, then coins

Sort the money from biggest to smallest. Count the dollars, then count on the cents.

Example

Count 5 quarters and 3 dimes.

25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢, 125¢, then 135¢, 145¢, 155¢. 155¢ = $1.55.

Answer: $1.55

Make an amount with the fewest coins and bills

$1.35 can be a loonie, a quarter and a dime, or 5 quarters and a dime, and more. For the fewest coins and bills, use the biggest one you can each time.

Make change by counting up

Start at the price. Count up to the next 10¢, then to the next dollar, then to the money paid. Add the jumps.

Example

A backpack costs $27.95. Pay with a $50 bill. What is the change?

$27.95 + 5¢ = $28. $28 + $2 = $30. $30 + $20 = $50. 5¢ + $2 + $20 = $22.05. Check: $27.95 + $22.05 = $50.

Answer: $22.05

Cash rounding

There are no pennies, so a cash total is rounded to the nearest 5¢. A card payment (debit or credit) is not rounded.

Total ends inCash roundingExample
1 or 2down to 0$3.42 → $3.40
3 or 4up to 5$3.43 → $3.45
6 or 7down to 5$3.47 → $3.45
8 or 9up to the next 10$3.48 → $3.50
0 or 5no change$3.45 stays $3.45

Simple money decisions

Better buy: find the cost of the same number of things. 4 juice boxes at $1.25 each cost $5, so a pack of 4 for $4 is the better buy. A bigger pack is not always cheaper, so always check.

Saving up: find how much more you need, then count by your savings. With $10 saved and $5 a week, a $45 item needs $35 more: 7 weeks.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
5 coins, so 5¢Count the value of each coin: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢, 70¢
A quarter is 20¢A quarter is 25¢. Four quarters make $1
5 quarters and 3 dimes is 55¢155¢ is $1.55. Do not lose the dollar
$10 − $7.65 = $3.35Count up: 5¢ + 30¢ + $2 = $2.35. One dollar was used to make the cents
Cash change from $10 for $7.48 is $2.52Round first: $7.48 → $7.50 in cash, so the change is $2.50

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about money in BC?
faq.a: The BC Grade 4 math curriculum includes financial literacy: monetary calculations, including making change with amounts to $100, and making simple financial decisions. Students count coins and bills, make change by counting up, and compare prices.

faq.q: How does cash rounding work in Canada?
faq.a: Canada no longer uses pennies, so cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢: amounts ending in 1 or 2 round down, 3 or 4 round up to 5, 6 or 7 round down to 5, and 8 or 9 round up. Debit and credit card payments are charged the exact amount.

faq.q: How do you teach making change in Grade 4?
faq.a: Count up from the price to the money paid: for $7.65 from $10, go to $7.70 (5¢), to $8 (30¢), then to $10 ($2), so the change is $2.35. Then check that price + change = money paid.

faq.q: Is money on the Grade 4 FSA?
faq.a: The FSA numeracy section is based on the BC curriculum, which includes financial literacy, so money can appear in word problems. Counting money and making change also practise the adding and subtracting with decimals that students use throughout the test.

items.q: Which money makes $2.40?

items.e: Four quarters make $1. $3 is 3 dollars, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 quarters. 15 would be right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 85¢?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 25¢, 25¢, 25¢, 10¢ = 85¢. That is 4 coins. Three quarters make 75¢. Add a dime: 85¢. Using dimes and nickels takes more coins.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?

items.q: How many dimes make $2.50?

sets.title: Cash rounding to the nearest 5¢ (card is exact)

items.q: A total of $3.47 is paid in cash. What is the cash total?
items.e: Canada has no pennies, so a cash total is rounded to the nearest 5¢. Last digit 1 or 2: round down to 0. 3 or 4: up to 5. 6 or 7: down to 5. 8 or 9: up to the next 10. $3.47 ends in 7, so it rounds down to $3.45. $3.50 rounds to the nearest 10¢, but cash rounds to the nearest 5¢.

items.q: Which total stays the same when it is paid in cash?
items.e: A total that already ends in 0 or 5 does not change. $4.35 ends in 5. $4.36 becomes $4.35, $4.38 becomes $4.40 and $4.31 becomes $4.30.

items.e: Round first: $11.57 ends in 7, so the cash total is $11.55. Count up from $11.55 to $20: $11.55 + 5¢ = $11.60, $11.60 + 40¢ = $12, $12 + $8 = $20. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 40¢ + $8 = $8.45. The change is $8.45. $8.43 forgets to round the total.

items.q: Mateo’s total is $36.51. He pays cash with a $50 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Round first: $36.51 ends in 1, so the cash total is $36.50. Count up from $36.50 to $50: $36.50 + 50¢ = $37, $37 + $3 = $40, $40 + $10 = $50. Add the jumps: 50¢ + $3 + $10 = $13.50. The change is $13.50. $13.49 forgets to round the total.

items.q: Ryan’s total is $73.19. He pays cash with a $100 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Round first: $73.19 ends in 9, so the cash total is $73.20. Count up from $73.20 to $100: $73.20 + 80¢ = $74, $74 + $6 = $80, $80 + $20 = $100. Add the jumps: 80¢ + $6 + $20 = $26.80. The change is $26.80. $26.81 forgets to round the total.

items.q: A total is $9.92. How much less does Mei pay with cash than by card?
items.e: By card: exactly $9.92. In cash: $9.92 ends in 2, so it rounds down to $9.90. $9.92 − $9.90 = 2¢ less. 8¢ comes from rounding up to $10.

items.q: A total is $6.38. How much more does Wei pay with cash than by card?
items.e: By card: exactly $6.38. In cash: $6.38 ends in 8, so it rounds up to $6.40. $6.40 − $6.38 = 2¢ more. 3¢ comes from rounding down to $6.35.

sets.title: Better buys, saving up and word problems

items.q: Juice boxes cost $1.25 each, or $4 for a pack of 4. Leah needs 4 juice boxes. Which is the better buy?
items.e: 4 single boxes: $1.25 + $1.25 + $1.25 + $1.25 = $5. The pack costs $4. The pack of 4 saves $1.

items.q: At the Kelowna farmers’ market, peaches are $1.75 each or 2 for $3. Simran wants 2 peaches. Which is the better buy?
items.e: 2 peaches at $1.75 each: $1.75 + $1.75 = $3.50. 2 for $3 costs $3. 2 for $3 saves 50¢.

items.q: Tennis balls cost $1.50 each, or $5 for a can of 3. Sofia needs 3 balls. Which is the better buy?
items.e: 3 single balls: $1.50 + $1.50 + $1.50 = $4.50. The can costs $5. 3 single balls cost 50¢ less. A bigger pack is not always cheaper.

items.q: Hockey cards come in a pack of 10 for $5 or a box of 30 for $12. Owen wants 30 cards. Which is the better buy?
items.e: 30 cards is 3 packs: $5 + $5 + $5 = $15. The box costs $12. The box of 30 saves $3. 1 pack of 10 is cheaper, but it has only 10 cards.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Ji-woo collects $5, $10, $2.50 and $1.75. How much does she collect in all?
Lucas wants a lacrosse stick that costs $45. He saves $5 each week. How many weeks will it take?
Liam has $10. He saves $5 each week for a $45 skateboard helmet. How many more weeks until he can buy it?
items.e: He needs $45 − $10 = $35 more. Count by 5s to 35: 7 jumps. That is 7 weeks. 9 weeks forgets the $10 he already has.

items.q: Olivia wants a pair of hiking boots for $45. She has $28. How much more money does she need?
items.e: Count up: $28 + $2 = $30, $30 + $15 = $45. $2 + $15 = $17, so she needs $17 more. $23 takes the smaller digit from the bigger one. $15 forgets the jump from $28 to $30. $73 adds.

items.q: Harjot saves $6 each week for a $45 soccer ball and jersey. How many weeks until he has enough?
items.e: After 7 weeks: 7 × $6 = $42. That is not enough. After 8 weeks: 8 × $6 = $48. So it takes 8 weeks. 7 weeks leaves Harjot $3 short.

items.q: Hana has $18. A bike light costs $30. She saves $4 each week. After how many weeks can she buy the light?
items.e: She needs $30 − $18 = $12 more. $4, $8, $12: that is 3 weeks. 12 is the dollars, not the weeks.

items.q: On a class trip to Grouse Mountain, Ava has $20. She buys lunch for $8.75 and a postcard set for $6.50. How much money is left?
Nadia has $12. She wants a book for $7.95 and a bookmark for $3.50. Does she have enough money?
items.e: $7.95 + $3.50: $7.95 + 5¢ = $8, and $8 + $3.45 = $11.45. $11.45 is less than $12. $11.45 + 55¢ = $12, so yes, with 55¢ left. $1.55 comes from adding the cents without making a new dollar.

items.q: Jasleen has $20. Which 2 items can she buy?
items.e: Sketchbook and brushes: $9.50 + $6.40 = $15.90, less than $20. Sketchbook and paint set: $22.25. Brushes and easel: $23.20. Paint set and easel: $29.55.

items.q: A rain jacket costs $40 at one store, with $10 off. Another store sells it for $32. Where should Ethan buy it?
items.e: $40 − $10 = $30. $30 is less than $32, so the store with $10 off is cheaper by $2.

items.q: On the ferry to Vancouver Island, Arjun buys a sandwich for $6.85 and a juice for $2.40. He pays with a $20 bill. How much change does he get?
items.e: Cost: $6.85 + $2.40 = $9.25. Count up from $9.25 to $20: $9.25 + 5¢ = $9.30, $9.30 + 70¢ = $10, $10 + $10 = $20. Add the jumps: 5¢ + 70¢ + $10 = $10.75. The change is $10.75. $11.75 forgets the dollar used for the cents.

items.q: Kai gets $6 each week. He saves half and spends half. How much does he save in 4 weeks?
items.e: Half of $6 is $3. 4 weeks: $3 + $3 + $3 + $3 = $12. $24 is all the money, not half of it.

items.q: At an Okanagan fruit stand, Zara buys cherries for $7.38. She pays cash with a $10 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Cash: $7.38 rounds up to $7.40. Count up from $7.40 to $10: $7.40 + 60¢ = $8, $8 + $2 = $10. Add the jumps: 60¢ + $2 = $2.60. The change is $2.60. $2.62 forgets to round the total.

items.q: The bus for a field trip to Stanley Park costs $4 for each student. 23 students go. What is the total cost?
items.e: 23 × $4: 20 × $4 = $80 and 3 × $4 = $12. $80 + $12 = $92. $83 multiplies only the tens. $27 adds instead of multiplying.

items.q: Chloe pays for rain boots that cost $44.95 with three $20 bills. How much change does she get?
items.e: Three $20 bills make $60. Count up from $44.95 to $60: $44.95 + 5¢ = $45, $45 + $5 = $50, $50 + $10 = $60. Add the jumps: 5¢ + $5 + $10 = $15.05. The change is $15.05. $16.05 forgets the dollar used for the cents.

items.q: Noah has $20 and gets $5 each week. He wants a $40 game. If he spends nothing, after how many weeks can he buy it?
items.e: He needs $40 − $20 = $20 more. $5, $10, $15, $20: that is 4 weeks. 8 weeks forgets the $20 he already has.
